title: Keeping hope
hookLine: hope stays in Pandora's jar: Dickinson's bird with feathers, or Seneca's chain to fear?
tomorrow: what did a grieving father in the Qur'an call his patience?

cards: Some people check the forecast ten times before a trip; others refuse to look at all, so they can't be let down. The Greek poet Hesiod tells an old story about that.
Pandora lifts the lid of a great jar, and out fly troubles and sicknesses, into the world. She claps the lid back down. One thing is left inside, under the rim, and it doesn't fly out.
Hope. Hesiod says only that the lid came down first, by the will of Zeus. What hope is doing in there, he never says.

teach.b: So is hope the last gift, kept safe for us? Or one more trouble, still in the jar? Readers split, and both sides have a real case.
The first side: hope is the good thing that stayed.
Emily Dickinson wrote it as a small bird: "the thing with feathers / That perches in the soul." It sings in the worst storm, she says, and it never once asked her for a crumb.

On this view hope is a gift you don't have to earn, and it keeps you alive. The second side is Stoic. Seneca, writing to his friend Lucilius, quotes the Stoic Hecato: stop hoping, and you'll stop fearing.

Hope and fear, Seneca says, are chained together like a prisoner and the soldier who guards him; where one walks, the other walks too. On this view hope drags you out of today into a future you don't control.
Put both in a hospital room. One voice says: keep the bird singing; don't let him give up. The other says: don't hang him on a promise; help him live this day.
One small surprise: in Hesiod, it's a jar, not a box.
The Stoics wanted the mind here, on what's yours to do. Dickinson's bird doesn't promise an outcome either. It just keeps singing.

how: Hesiod's Works and Days tells of the jar with hope left inside, and readers still argue whether hope is a blessing or a trouble. Dickinson's 'the thing with feathers' and Seneca's fifth letter are often read side by side as the two views.

o: holding a hope lightly, without staking all on one outcome
insisting things will turn out fine no matter what happens
giving up on wanting anything so nothing can hurt

games.q: the jar and the bird: tap the pairs.
p: lifts the lid of the great jar

s: in Hesiod, Pandora opens a box
Hesiod's story has a great jar.
Hesiod says plainly whether hope is a blessing or a curse
he says the lid came down by Zeus's will, but never what hope means there; readers have argued both ways.
Seneca links hope and fear together
like a prisoner chained to the soldier who guards him.

games.q: a friend's dad has a scan next week. he says, "i'm not getting my hopes up." what's the best case for his view?
o: hope and fear are chained: hoping hard for one result means dreading the other.
hope is bad luck: expecting good news makes bad news more likely.
hope belongs only to religious people; without God there's nothing to hope in.
games.why: that's Seneca's case, from the Stoic Hecato: stop hoping and you'll stop fearing. Dickinson's answer is the bird that sings anyway.

practice: Name one hope out loud, in a single sentence. Then name one small piece of it that's yours to do today. Hold both together, the bird and the task, and let the breath come and go.

wordCard.voice: Keeping hope: letting the bird sing without hanging everything on one outcome. Dickinson's feathers, and Seneca's warning.

orig.note: Greek: hope, the thing left in Pandora's jar in Hesiod.

carryVoice: Your line: feathers. A small bird that sings in the storm and asks nothing back. Talk soon.
